newsitem.title: UK: Trade jitters nudge dollar/yen into spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Trade jitters nudge dollar/yen into spotlight.

text.p: Dollar/yen was nudging dollar/mark out of the limelight in early Europe as market thoughts turned from EMU to the U.S./Japan trade gap.
The deal reached by EU leaders Monday on the stability pact, designed to keep budget deficits down after EMU begins, kept the mark under broad-based pressure and boosted dollar/mark.

But dollar/yen was fighting to stay steady as players looked ahead to tonight's Japanese May trade data -- expected to show a growing surplus -- and Thursday's U.S. April numbers, where the complete opposite, a worsening deficit, is expected.
All this has added piquancy ahead of the looming G7 summit.
The Group of Seven meet in Denver, Colorado on June 20-22, and the market fears that the expanding trade gap will see sparks fly between the U.S. and Japan.
Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered, said the U.S. was indeed concerned about trade but not to the point that they were willing to engage heavily in exchange rate rhetoric.
"The issue is to try to get Japan to boost demand and how they do that, rather than by trying to engineer a manipulation of exchange rates," said Fox.
Japan's May trade surplus, to be revealed at 2350 GMT, is forecast to grow to 549 billion yen from 229 billion in April.
The U.S. April deficit, by contrast, is seen widening to $10 billion from $8.5 billion in March.
The dollar slipped to 113.18/28 yen by 0747 GMT from late Monday's European level 113.45/55.
Dollar/mark rose to 1.7345/50 from 1.7295/05.
The general strength of the yen and weakness of the mark saw the mark/yen cross slide to 65.28/31 from Monday's 65.63/66.

The agreement on the budget stability pact hammered out by EU leaders on Monday at their Amsterdam summit -- which concludes today -- should continue to buoy dollar/mark as it increases the risk of a weak single currency, analysts said.

The deal included a resolution on jobs and growth, taking account of French concerns, but analysts warned that it had not destroyed the potential for future conflict between France and Germany -- nor the risk of EMU delay.
Fears monetary union will be postponed usually boost the mark as the market prices in a reduced risk that the German currency will be subsumed into a weaker euro.

"The compromise does highlight a fundamentally different vision of the future European currency in Paris and Bonn which may cause future problems," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America in London.

Today sees a raft of data releases from the United States, foremost among them May CPI at 1230 GMT. Economists expect rises of 0.2 percent on the month and 2.4 percent year-on-year compared to April's 0.1 and 2.5 percent increases.

The market is looking for subdued inflation, after data out Friday showed a surprise fall in May producer prices and dampened speculation that the Federal Reserve would tighten at its next policy-making meeting on July 1-2.
"The risk is of a small (CPI) rise but not to the extent that it would reverse last week's prognosis, that rates aren't going to change in July," said Fox at Standard Chartered.
U.S. May housing starts are also due at 1230 GMT, while industrial production and capacity utilization follow at 1315 GMT and real earnings at 1400 GMT.
Data out from the UK revealed a public sector deficit of 3.96 billion stg in May, bigger than the consensus market forecast of 2.9 billion. April had seen a surprise debt repayment.
Sterling was quoted at 2.8370/80 marks and $1.6336/47 at 0850 GMT compared to 2.8295/05 and $1.6349/54 in late Europe on Monday.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
